expectations.text: Output flags that the 'same items for everyone therefore items are fixed' reasoning is incorrect
expectations.evidence: "Even though you *chose* these 48 images deliberately, they still introduce variance... The selection mechanism (deliberate vs. random sampling) is separate from whether image-level variance needs to be partitioned out. It does."

expectations.text: Output explains that items should be treated as random because the researcher wants to generalize beyond these specific 48 images to the population of similar stimuli — which requires treating items as a random sample
expectations.evidence: The response frames the issue as variance inflation and anti-conservative tests ('collapses into the residual, inflating your effective sample size'), not as a generalizability argument. It never explicitly states that treating items as random is required for conclusions to generalize beyond these 48 specific images to a broader population of similar stimuli.

expectations.text: Output recommends adding by-item random effects — (1 | item) at minimum, and by-item random slopes for within-item conditions if applicable
expectations.evidence: "Minimum recommended model: lmer(rating ~ condition + (1 | subject) + (1 | image))" and later discusses when `(condition | image)` would be appropriate if images appear in multiple conditions.

expectations.text: Output does NOT validate the advisor's framing or agree that fixed-item analysis is appropriate
expectations.evidence: While the response says "Your advisor is right that (1 | subject) is necessary," it immediately adds "but the model as specified has a meaningful gap" and clearly states the advisor's implied conclusion (that the model is sufficient) is wrong, recommending the addition of image random effects.

expectations.text: Output references Clark (1973) / language-as-fixed-effect fallacy, OR Judd et al., OR explains that treating items as fixed means conclusions don't generalize beyond those 48 specific images
expectations.evidence: "This is the stimuli-as-fixed-effect fallacy (Clark, 1973; Judd, Westfall & Kenny, 2012)" and both Clark (1973) and Judd et al. (2012) are listed in the key references section.
